case_study_insert.main_stem: Foxglove Pet Supplies (FPS) is a private limited company in the online pet food and supplies retail sector, employing a workforce of 45. Founded in 2019 by Priya Nandakumar in Dunmarrow, the business sells pet food, toys and accessories online with two stores and operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. FPS plans to invest $535,000 in an automated subscription fulfilment kitchen and a second store, financed by $310,000 hire purchase for the packing line and $225,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $96,000 a year, a variable cost of $14 a unit and a selling price of $20, and currently produces 24,500 units a year. FPS faces a growing operational problem: packing staff turnover has reached 18% and short or incorrect shipments persist.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — September 2026: The subscription fulfilment kitchen packed 14,200 orders last quarter; 4.4% of shipments were short or incorrect, down from 6.8% a year ago. A survey of 700 subscribers found 57% want a wider grain-free range, 49% would bundle toys with food deliveries, and average basket value is $46. Next-day delivery covers 92% of orders. Customer complaints fell from 61 to 40 per month. Off-the-job training at the Dunmarrow logistics college costs $650 per employee, while on-the-job coaching is led by shift supervisors.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Foxglove Pet Supplies as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, making variable-rate borrowing and hire purchase more expensive. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.9% from $11.60 to $12.40 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills for hourly-paid packing and delivery staff. (3) Pet food ingredient costs (poultry and cereals) rose 11.5% year-on-year, inflation is running at 3.8%, and online pet product spending grew 6.4% in the same period.

questions.question_text: FPS plans to finance its $535,000 expansion partly with hire purchase. Explain two advantages for FPS of using hire purchase for the packing line rather than a bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $310,000 cost of the packing line across its working life, matching payments to the revenue the line will generate from the 14,200 orders it helps pack each quarter. FPS keeps its cash buffer intact, vital when 4.4% of shipments are still short or incorrect and complaints, though down from 61 to 40 per month, keep arriving; the $225,000 of retained profit can then stay available to stabilise operations rather than being swallowed by one asset purchase.

Point 2: Hire purchase agreements usually secure onto the equipment itself, so it can be simpler to arrange than a further bank loan when the base rate sits at 5.25%. Interest is fixed in the agreement, giving FPS certainty for budgeting the automated kitchen and second store, no surprises if rates rise again, and full ownership of the line at the end of the term, after which maintenance and staffing savings can be redirected into the subscription growth its members support, 57% of whom want a wider grain-free range and 49% of whom would bundle toys with food deliveries.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of hire purchase identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Foxglove Pet Supplies and its subscription expansion.

questions.question_text: FPS is launching its subscription bundle. Consider paid social media advertising, influencer marketing with pet creators, or local radio sponsorship. Which should FPS choose to promote the subscription? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Paid social media advertising: Paid social lets FPS target lookalike audiences built from its 700 surveyed subscribers, retarget abandoned baskets, and push the bundle (food plus toy bundling appeals to 49% of subscribers) at low cost per click. It is measurable and fast to set up, but feeds are competitive, creative must be refreshed constantly, and subscription intent is hard to read from a cold ad alone.

Influencer marketing with pet creators: Partnering with pet creators reaches exactly the 57% of subscribers wanting a wider grain-free range and the 49% interested in toy bundles, with trusted, authentic content; unboxing videos of the fulfilment kitchen convert strongly in pet communities, and creators can demonstrate the actual box contents and next-day feel. Results depend on creator fit, disclosure and consistency beyond launch week.

Local radio sponsorship: Radio is cheap and local to Dunmarrow and reinforces brand familiarity for the two stores, and it can repeat a memorable subscription offer to commuters. But it cannot visualise the product, skews toward older listeners, and lacks a direct, trackable path to online subscription sign-up, which is FPS's growth engine and where 92% next-day coverage already applies.

Recommendation: FPS should choose influencer marketing with pet creators. It matches the research, fits the pet-community channel where subscription decisions are made, and scales cost with results rather than fixed airtime. Paid social is rejected as a follower rather than a leader; boosting creator posts should come second. Local radio is rejected as untargeted and unable to demonstrate the subscription offer or produce a measurable sign-up, so it cannot lead a digital-first launch.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal application to FPS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of FPS with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of FPS with a well-justified recommendation explaining why paid social alone and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: FPS packing staff turnover has reached 18%. Explain two advantages for FPS of its laissez-faire leadership style for the packing team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives experienced packers the autonomy to organise their own pick-pack-seal routines around the 4.4% error problem, tapping operator knowledge rather than handed-down redesign. Skilled staff experimenting privately often build the fastest workflows, lifting both speed and accuracy without capital spend, and the calm, trusting environment suits a small 45-person team that cross-covers two stores and the fulfilment kitchen.

Point 2: Trust and autonomy raise morale and reduce friction for a group with 18% staff turnover, making FPS a more attractive employer than rigidly controlled warehouses. Autonomy also lets shift supervisors coach informally on the floor, which pairs naturally with the on-the-job route already in place, and it protects the 92% next-day coverage because motivated self-starters keep dispatch flowing during subscription peaks. The risk is drift into sloppy practice, so FPS must keep the short-or-incorrect shipment metric visible on the wall and step in decisively when standards slip, or the 4.4% error rate will creep back toward 6.8%.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of laissez-faire leadership identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to FPS's turnover, error rate and packing environment.

questions.question_text: FPS wants to cut short or incorrect shipments (4.4%) further. Consider on-the-job coaching by shift supervisors or off-the-job training at the Dunmarrow logistics college. Which should FPS choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job coaching: Supervisor-led coaching is embedded in the live pick-pack-seal flow, so the 4.4% error rate can be targeted at the exact failure points, wrong item, wrong quantity, missing treats or broken seals. It is immediate, specific to FPS's SOPs and equipment, and free in course fees, protecting the 92% next-day delivery promise across 14,200 orders a quarter. Weaknesses are that supervisors lose picking time and that quality and patience vary between coaches, so FPS should give them a simple checklist and short calibration sessions.

Off-the-job training: The college's $650 per employee course covers warehouse standards, scanning discipline and health-and-safety with certification, which would formalise FPS's processes and give a recognised credential for external recognition. Training all 45 employees would cost $29,250 (45 x $650) plus absence cover, a heavy sum at a moment when FPS is also absorbing hire-purchase repayments on $310,000 of equipment and cash fell from $55,000 to $40,000; cover for packers would be hard to find during the subscription peak. Content is generic and would still need adaptation to the Dunmarrow kitchen layout.

Decision: FPS should choose on-the-job coaching as the primary route, sending shift leads to the college to standardise their coaching. It is specific, immediate and fee-free, directly attacking the 4.4% error rate without stripping the packing line during peak subscription weeks. Full off-the-job training for the whole workforce is rejected because $29,250 plus cover costs strain cash precisely when liquidity has tightened, and generic modules would need customising to FPS's SOPs anyway; leads can then cascade the same checklist back to their crews.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to FPS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of FPS.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of FPS with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and error-reduction relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how FPS's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs / Contribution per unit. Substitution: $96,000 / ($20 - $14) = $96,000 / $6 = 16,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 16,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price - Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $20 - $14 = $6. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways FPS's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. FPS can compare break-even output of 16,000 units with actual output of 24,500 units, showing a margin of safety of 8,500 units (34.7% of output), which supports scaling the subscription kitchen rather than cutting it back.
2. The $6 contribution per unit lets managers test the economics of the $46 average basket; if a food-plus-toys bundle lifts the basket to $56 while variable cost rises only $2 (to $16), contribution becomes $10, so managers can price the bundle confidently.
3. Knowing break-even output helps FPS time hire-purchase repayments on the $310,000 packing line; each additional 1,000 units sold adds $6,000 of contribution, so managers can model how many extra subscription orders are needed to cover the line before signing off further capacity or a third store.
4. Managers can use productivity data (24,500 units / 45 employees = 544.4 units per employee) to set packing targets, identify under-performing shifts driving the 4.4% error rate, and decide whether rota or layout changes can absorb peak volumes without extra hires.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 16,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety vs 24,500-unit output; bundle pricing maths on the $46 basket; hire-purchase phasing against break-even; and productivity of 544.4 units per employee to plan packing shifts.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate FPS's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has FPS's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.42 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.13 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.70 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.59 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $120,000 inventories + $60,000 trade receivables + $55,000 cash = $235,000; 2025 current assets = $105,000 + $75,000 + $40,000 = $220,000. Ratio 2024 = $235,000 / $165,000 = 1.42; 2025 = $220,000 / $195,000 = 1.13. Excluding inventories: 2024 = ($235,000 - $120,000) / $165,000 = $115,000 / $165,000 = 0.70; 2025 = ($220,000 - $105,000) / $195,000 = $115,000 / $195,000 = 0.59.

Evaluation: Liquidity has weakened. The coverage of current assets over current liabilities fell from 1.42 to 1.13 and the quick measure excluding inventories fell from 0.70 to 0.59. Cash declined from $55,000 to $40,000 while current liabilities rose from $165,000 to $195,000 (partly to fund the $310,000 hire-purchase-funded automation and the second store), and trade receivables crept up from $60,000 to $75,000. Inventories fell from $120,000 to $105,000, which is lean and reduces write-off risk on pet food, but it did not offset the liability growth.

Conclusion: FPS's financial position has not improved; it has deteriorated. Both the current ratio (1.42 to 1.13) and the acid test ratio (0.70 to 0.59) show tighter short-term solvency, and even though the $535,000 expansion grew non-current assets from $720,000 to $980,000, it has been financed with debt and working-capital strain rather than matching internal cash generation. Before the second store opens, FPS should pause further commitments, tighten receivables, extend supplier terms where possible, and confirm subscription cash inflows cover the hire-purchase instalments with room to spare.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables, cash and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether FPS's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for FPS of promoting a grain-free subscription bundle to its subscribers.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: 57% of the 700 surveyed subscribers want a wider grain-free range, so a grain-free bundle attacks proven latent demand rather than a guess, lifting average basket value above the current $46 and deepening subscription stickiness. Monthly recurring revenue smooths FPS's lumpy cash cycle, suits the automated fulfilment kitchen, and defends the 92% next-day delivery coverage promise that keeps members from straying to big-box rivals; bundling toys alongside grain-free food also plays to the 49% who would buy such bundles, widening revenue per shipment without new customers.

Disadvantage: Grain-free ingredients cost more than standard poultry and cereal recipes, pushing up the $14 variable cost per unit and pressuring the already-thin contribution at precisely the moment ingredient costs are up 11.5% year-on-year. If the bundle fails quality checks or sells unevenly, the 4.4% short-or-incorrect rate worsens, margins are squeezed on every unit, and the stock risk rises; FPS may also find the 57% who want grain-free products are price-sensitive, so aggressive subscription discounting to win them could destroy the $46 basket economics before the second store even opens.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to FPS's subscriber research, ingredient costs and error rate.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.9% minimum wage increase and the 11.5% rise in pet food ingredient costs will affect FPS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If FPS's $310,000 hire purchase is variable-rate, each 0.25% adds 0.0025 x $310,000 = $775 a year, so the full 0.75% rise adds about $2,325 a year (0.0075 x $310,000). That is manageable in isolation, but combined with repayments it tightens a cash position that has already fallen to $40,000 in the 2025 extract and pushes up the cost of any future overdraft or second-store borrowing; fixing the rate or negotiating hire-purchase terms now is prudent.

Minimum wage increase (6.9%, to $12.40 per hour): FPS's packing and delivery teams include hourly-paid staff, so the rise is compulsory and recurring. No hours or pay rates are stated in the insert, so no defensible annual total can be invented; at productivity of 24,500 units / 45 employees = 544.4 units per employee, the cost is absorbable only if the 4.4% error rate keeps falling and throughput rises, otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $14 variable cost effectively increases, squeezing contribution per unit.

Ingredient cost inflation (11.5% poultry and cereals): As an explicit upper bound, if the full $14 variable cost rose with ingredient inflation it would add $1.61 per unit (0.115 x $14); across 24,500 units that is about $39,445 a year (24,500 x $1.61 = $39,445). Even partial pass-through erodes the $6 contribution toward roughly $4.39, and pet-owner price sensitivity limits how far subscriptions can be repriced, though 6.4% growth in online pet spending and the 57% grain-free demand give room on premium lines.

Conclusion: The 11.5% rise in pet food ingredient costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 24,500 units sold, unlike the capped $2,325 annual interest effect or the productivity-contingent wage rise. FPS should re-price the grain-free premium range, lock in annual supplier contracts, keep the $225,000 retained-profit buffer intact, and monitor liquidity before committing to any further expansion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to FPS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on FPS's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of FPS with a well-justified judgement that ingredient-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
